title: WKWebView and JavaScript bridges
summary: `WKWebView` shows web content inside your app. The app and the page can talk through message handlers (JS → native) and `evaluateJavaScript` (native → JS).
body: **In simple words:** Some screens (help pages, promotions, checkout) are built on the web and shown inside the app with `WKWebView`. It runs the page in a separate process, so a crashing page does not crash your app.

**JS → native:** register `WKScriptMessageHandler` with a name; the page calls `window.webkit.messageHandlers.<name>.postMessage(data)`. **Native → JS:** `webView.evaluateJavaScript("...")` or `callAsyncJavaScript`.
**Control navigation:** `WKNavigationDelegate.decidePolicyFor` lets you block or open links externally and intercept deep links.
**Cookies and login:** share session via `WKWebsiteDataStore.httpCookieStore`. Note it is separate from `HTTPCookieStorage.shared`.
**Security:** only allow trusted domains, validate every message from JS (treat as untrusted input), never expose sensitive native APIs broadly, and avoid `loadHTMLString` with untrusted content.
**Retain cycle trap:** `userContentController.add(self, name:)` holds `self` strongly; remove the handler on teardown or use a weak proxy.
**Alternatives:** `SFSafariViewController` for showing external sites with Safari features and shared cookies (no control over content); SwiftUI `WebView` (iOS 26).
keyPoints: WKWebView runs out of process; use delegates to control navigation.
Bridge: message handlers (JS → native) and evaluateJavaScript (native → JS).
Treat all JS messages as untrusted; allow-list domains.
Message handlers retain their target - remove them to avoid leaks.

mistakes: Not checking the origin of JS messages.
followups: **Native vs web screen - how do you decide?** Web for frequently changing content and shared flows across platforms; native for performance, offline use and platform integration.
